The Game Plan: Brainstorming Data Analysis

Welcome back, everyone! While you were all getting set up, I asked you to download an Excel spreadsheet containing some experimental data (if you haven’t yet, grab it here: https://tinyurl.com/N2314-260909-data). This file contains temperature versus time measurements of hot tea cooling down, collected by four different teams in our lab.

Before we jump into the software, we need a game plan. I always like to spend a minute or two just looking at the raw numbers and brainstorming. What kind of useful information can we extract from this? How should we graph it?

A few of you had some great ideas right out of the gate:

  • Individual vs. Overlay Plots: We could make four separate graphs, one for each team. But as a few of you pointed out, overlaying all four data series onto a single graph makes it much easier to visually compare the cooling behaviors side-by-side.

  • Temperature vs. Temperature Difference: We could plot the raw temperature, T, against time, t. Alternatively, we could plot the change in temperature relative to the room, \Delta T = T - T_a, where T_a is the ambient temperature.

  • Averaging: Since all teams presumably ran the experiment under very similar conditions (same ambient temperature, roughly the same volume of water), we could average the four data series together to get a more robust dataset.

There was one slight hiccup in the raw data—Team 1 was missing their water depth measurement. Thanks to the team members who chimed in, we now know it was 2.0 inches. We will definitely want to keep track of that depth parameter, as it might reveal some interesting physics later on.

Teaming Up with AI in Google Colab

For the rest of today, we are going to analyze this dataset like pros. Go ahead and open up a fresh Google Colab notebook. We will be relying on Google’s Gemini AI to write the Python code for us, but remember: the AI is only as smart as the instructions we give it. It is entirely up to us to tell it exactly what we want.

First, we need to upload our Excel file to the Colab environment so the AI can actually see it. Once that is done, we write our first prompt. You don’t have to be overly formal, but you do need to be explicit about the data structure. I told Gemini:

"Attached is an Excel data file showing temperature versus time of hot cups of water measured by 4 different teams. Each sheet has data for one team (4 sheets total). The 1st column is time in minutes, the 2nd column is temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, and the 4th column has water depth."

Even without asking it to plot anything yet, Gemini is usually smart enough to import the pandas library and load the data, as shown below.

Now, let’s ask it for our first graph: "Please plot one graph that shows temperature versus time for all four teams."

When you run the generated code, you might get a plot with lines connecting every single data point. Personally, I am not a fan of that look for raw experimental data. Connecting the dots implies that we know exactly what the temperature was between our measurements, which we don’t. It makes the graph look like a continuous simulation rather than discrete experimental observations.

Let’s refine our prompt to fix this: "Show each data point as a discrete symbol. Use a different color and shape for each team. Do not have lines connecting adjacent data points."

Mathematical Modeling: Fitting the Curve

Plotting the raw data is nice, but what is a computer program really good for? Finding the overall trend by fitting the data to a mathematical model.

Looking at the scatter plot, the temperature drops off quickly at first and then gradually levels out. This is a classic signature of exponential decay. So, let’s tell the AI to fit our data to an exponential function.

If we are not careful, we might suggest a model that looks like this: \begin{equation} T(t) = C e^{-rt} \tag{1} \end{equation} where T(t) is the temperature at time t, C is a scaling constant, and r is the decay rate.

If you ask the AI to fit this exact equation to the raw temperature data, the resulting curve will look terrible. Why? Because Equation 1 assumes that as time t \to \infty, the temperature T will decay all the way down to zero. Unless we are conducting this experiment in a freezer at absolute zero, our tea is not going to reach zero degrees. It will only cool down to the ambient room temperature.

To fix this, we must elevate our model so that it sits on top of the ambient temperature, T_a. We know our room was sitting at 76^\circ\text{F}. Therefore, the correct physical model is: \begin{equation} T(t) = C e^{-rt} + T_a \tag{2} \end{equation} Alternatively, we can subtract T_a from both sides to model the temperature difference, \Delta T: \begin{equation} \Delta T(t) = C e^{-rt} \tag{3} \end{equation}

In this model, we have two adjustable (or "fittable") parameters that the computer needs to figure out for us:

  • C: The initial temperature difference at t=0.

  • r: The decay rate, which tells us how rapidly the tea cools.

Let’s prompt Gemini to fit Equation 2 to our data. Because I am a stickler for proper scientific reporting, I am also going to demand that the AI includes the appropriate units for our parameters (^\circ\text{F} for C, and \text{min}^{-1} for r).

Furthermore, I want to see the error bars (the uncertainty) for these parameters. When you analyze data, your model almost never flawlessly matches your measurements. If a model hits every single data point dead-on, somebody probably faked the data! The numbers we extract for C and r are not exact; they exist within a confidence interval.

Extracting Physical Insights: Does Depth Matter?

Now we have some solid numbers. We thought all four teams were running the exact same experiment, but there was an accidental variation: the depth of the water in the cups varied from 2.0 inches to 2.7 inches.

Does the amount of water affect how fast the tea cools? We can investigate this by plotting our newly extracted decay rates (r) against the water depths.

Looking at this new graph, we see a potential pattern: the teams with shallower water (smaller volume) seem to have steeper, faster decay rates. This makes intuitive physical sense based on surface-area-to-volume ratios and thermal mass.

However, look closely at those error bars—especially for Team 1. The uncertainty is quite large. While the trend is suggestive, the error margins are wide enough that I wouldn’t rush to publish these results just yet. As a coach, my advice here would be to head back to the lab and run more trials at varying depths to tighten up those confidence intervals.

A New Perspective: The Power of Log Scales

While I was walking around the room, a student in the back showed me a graph their AI generated that looked entirely different. Instead of a declining curve, their data formed a straight line. The AI had gone a bit rogue and plotted the data on a logarithmic scale. Let’s talk about why that happens and why it is actually an incredibly powerful analytical tool.

Normally, we plot data on a linear scale. Every step up the y-axis represents adding a constant amount (e.g., +20^\circ\text{F}). But on a logarithmic scale, every step up the y-axis represents multiplying by a constant factor (usually a factor of 10).

Log scales are fantastic when your measurements span many orders of magnitude. Imagine you start with piping hot tea at \Delta T = 100^\circ\text{F}. As it cools, it might eventually reach \Delta T = 1^\circ\text{F}, and then \Delta T = 0.1^\circ\text{F}. On a standard linear graph, those late-stage measurements just look like zero—they get squashed against the bottom axis. A log scale stretches out the bottom end, allowing you to see the fine details of the cooling process even as the temperature difference becomes tiny.

But there is an even better mathematical reason to use a log scale. Let’s take our exponential model for the temperature difference (Equation 3) and apply the natural logarithm (\ln) to both sides: \begin{align} \ln(\Delta T) &= \ln\left(C e^{-rt}\right) \nonumber \\ \ln(\Delta T) &= \ln(C) + \ln\left(e^{-rt}\right) \nonumber \\ \ln(\Delta T) &= -rt + \ln(C) \tag{4} \end{align}

Does Equation 4 look familiar? It is the equation of a straight line, y = mx + b!

  • Our "y" variable is \ln(\Delta T).

  • Our slope "m" is the negative decay rate, -r.

  • Our "x" variable is time, t.

  • Our y-intercept "b" is \ln(C).

Here is the ultimate punchline: If you plot your data on a semi-log scale (log on the vertical, linear on the horizontal) and you see a linear trendline, the underlying physical behavior is exponential.

Let’s ask Gemini to recreate this view for our actual dataset by plotting \Delta T on a log scale.

Seeing those straight lines on the semi-log plot gives us immediate visual confirmation that our choice of an exponential decay model was the right call.
